rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metal ion is **not** coloured ?
rows.solution:
The ion that is NOT coloured is \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\).

Colour in a transition metal ion comes from a d-d transition: an electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper set. That requires the d subshell to be PARTLY filled — there must be an electron free to move and a vacancy for it to move into.

Copper is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^1\), so \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), formed by losing the single \(4s\) electron, is \(3d^{10}\): completely filled, with no vacancy anywhere in the set. No transition is possible, and its compounds are white.

The other three all have partly filled subshells — \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) is \(3d^7\), \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) is \(3d^2\) — and all three are coloured. Note that \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), at \(3d^9\), IS coloured; it is the \(+1\) state that is not.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following solutions will have the highest boiling point in water ?
rows.solution:
The highest boiling point belongs to the 1% CALCIUM CHLORIDE solution.

Elevation of boiling point is a colligative property: it depends on the NUMBER OF PARTICLES in solution, not on what they are. Each solution here holds 1 g of solute, so compare moles of particles per gram.

Calcium chloride dissociates into THREE ions and has a molar mass of 111, giving \(3/111 = 0{\cdot}027\) mol of particles per gram. Potassium chloride gives two ions from a molar mass of 74.5, so \(2/74{\cdot}5 = 0{\cdot}0268\) — very close, but just behind. Urea gives \(1/60 = 0{\cdot}0167\) and glucose only \(1/180 = 0{\cdot}0056\), both far below.

The two non-electrolytes are easily eliminated; the real contest is between the two salts, and calcium chloride wins on the extra ion.

rows.stem: During electrolysis of dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), using platinum electrodes, the gas evolved at the anode is :
rows.solution:
The gas evolved at the anode is OXYGEN.

The anode is where OXIDATION happens. In dilute sulphuric acid the two candidates are the sulphate ion and water, and water is oxidised far more readily — the sulphate ion is already at sulphur's highest oxidation state and its oxidation to peroxodisulphate needs a very high potential.

\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\)

Hydrogen is the trap: it IS evolved, but at the CATHODE, where reduction takes place. The question asks about the anode. Sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide would both require sulphate to be REDUCED, which cannot happen at an anode at all.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The activation energy \((\mathrm{E_a})\) of a reaction can be determined from the slope of which of the following plots ?
rows.solution:
The activation energy comes from the slope of \(\ln k\) against \(1/T\).

Take logarithms of the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\):
\(\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}\)

That is the equation of a straight line, \(y = c + mx\), provided \(y\) is \(\ln k\) and \(x\) is \(1/T\) — and only then. The slope is \(-E_a/R\), so \(E_a = -R \times \text{slope}\), and the intercept gives \(\ln A\).

Plotting \(\ln k\) against \(T\) itself gives a curve, not a line, so no slope can be read from it.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Which of the following represents the fraction of molecules with energies equal to or greater than \(\mathrm{E_a}\) ?
rows.solution:
The fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than \(E_a\) is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\).

It comes from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, and the form tells its own story. The exponent is NEGATIVE, so the fraction is always less than 1 — as it must be, being a fraction. Raise the temperature and \(E_a/RT\) shrinks, the exponent moves towards zero and the fraction RISES, which is why reactions go faster when heated. Raise the activation energy instead and the fraction falls.

The option with the positive exponent would exceed 1, which is impossible for a fraction; the two options without the exponential are the exponent itself, not the fraction.

rows.stem: The number of moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) precipitated when excess \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution is mixed with one mole of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\) is :
rows.solution:
NO precipitate is formed — 0 mol of silver chloride.

Silver nitrate precipitates only those chloride ions that are FREE IN SOLUTION, that is the ones outside the coordination sphere acting as counter ions. In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\) the square brackets close around ALL THREE chlorides: every one of them is a ligand bonded directly to cobalt, satisfying its secondary valence.

The complex is neutral overall — three ammonia molecules contribute nothing, three chlorido ligands give \(-3\), and cobalt is \(+3\) — so there is nothing outside the brackets at all, and nothing to ionise.

The same formula written as \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_2]Cl}\) would give 1 mol of precipitate, and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3]Cl_3}\) would give 3. What is precipitated counts what is OUTSIDE the brackets, never the total chlorine.

rows.stem: Which of the following haloalkanes react with aqueous KOH most rapidly by \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction ?
rows.solution:
2-BROMO-2-METHYLPROPANE reacts fastest by the unimolecular route.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set entirely by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step. 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is a TERTIARY halide, and its cation is stabilised by electron release from three methyl groups — the most stable of any offered here.

Of the others, 2-chlorobutane is secondary and gives a less stable cation; 1-bromobutane is primary; and 2,2-dimethyl-1-chloropropane, though it looks crowded, is also PRIMARY — its bulk sits on the neighbouring carbon, which hinders the bimolecular route without helping the unimolecular one.

Note that the bulk which blocks \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is exactly what favours \(\mathrm{S_N}1\), which is why the two orders run opposite to each other.

rows.stem:
The reaction
\(\mathrm{R-OH} + \mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RO^{-}Na^{+}} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2\,(g)}\)
suggests that alcohols are :
rows.solution:
The reaction shows that alcohols are ACIDIC.

Sodium metal displaces hydrogen from the alcohol, so what leaves the molecule is the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group as \(\mathrm{H^+}\) — the defining behaviour of a Bronsted acid. The alkoxide ion left behind is the conjugate base.

Sodium reacts the same way with water, which is the comparison to keep: alcohols are acids of the same family as water, merely WEAKER ones, because the alkyl group releases electron density and destabilises the alkoxide ion.

An alcohol can act as a base too, through the lone pairs on its oxygen — but this particular reaction is not the evidence for that.

rows.stem: At low temperature, phenol reacts with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) to form :
rows.solution:
At low temperature in carbon disulphide, phenol gives o- AND p-BROMOPHENOL — a mixture of the two MONObromo products.

The solvent is what decides. Carbon disulphide is non-polar, and the low temperature slows the substitution further, so bromination stops after ONE substitution and both activated positions are attacked, the para product predominating.

The contrast with bromine WATER is the point of the question. Water is polar; it helps the phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is even more strongly activating than phenol itself, and all three positions are then substituted at once to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate.

Same reagent, same substrate, two different products — the variable is the medium.

rows.stem: When alkyl iodide is treated with large excess of ammonia, the major product obtained is :
rows.solution:
With a LARGE EXCESS of ammonia the major product is the PRIMARY AMINE.

The difficulty with this reaction is that it does not stop. Ammonia attacks the alkyl iodide to give a primary amine, but that amine is itself a nucleophile — a better one than ammonia — so it attacks another molecule of the halide to give the secondary amine, and so on to the tertiary amine and finally the quaternary ammonium salt.

A large excess of ammonia solves it by PROBABILITY rather than by chemistry: with ammonia molecules vastly outnumbering the amine formed, any given halide molecule is overwhelmingly likely to meet ammonia first. The mixture still forms, but the primary amine dominates.

The opposite condition — excess alkyl halide — drives the sequence all the way to the quaternary salt.

rows.stem: An amine ‘X’ reacts with Hinsberg reagent and the product obtained is soluble in alkali. The amine ‘X’ is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — option (D) alone is printed as a DRAWN structure: a benzene ring bonded to \(-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CH_3}\). NAMED, not described: reading it as \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH-CH_3}\) is lossless and does NOT state the answer, because the answer is option (A) and the discrimination the question tests (primary vs secondary vs tertiary) survives intact — options (A), (B) and (C) are already printed as formulas. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The amine is METHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2}\).

Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, and the test turns on how many hydrogens remain on the nitrogen after it reacts.

A PRIMARY amine gives a sulphonamide that still has ONE hydrogen on its nitrogen. That hydrogen is made acidic by the two electron-withdrawing oxygens of the sulphonyl group beside it, so the product dissolves in alkali as its sodium salt — which is exactly what the question describes.

A SECONDARY amine gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on nitrogen, so it is insoluble in alkali; both dimethylamine and N-methylaniline fall here. A TERTIARY amine has no nitrogen-hydrogen bond to start with and does not react at all.

Alkali solubility therefore identifies a primary amine, and methylamine is the only one offered.

rows.stem: \(\alpha\)-helix structure refers to :
rows.solution:
The \(\alpha\)-helix is the SECONDARY structure of a protein.

The four levels are distinguished by what holds them together. The PRIMARY structure is the sequence of amino acid residues, fixed by peptide bonds. The SECONDARY structure is how the chain arranges itself locally in space — coiling into an \(\alpha\)-helix or folding into a \(\beta\)-pleated sheet — and is held by hydrogen bonds between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of one peptide linkage and the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) of another.

The TERTIARY structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain, and the QUATERNARY structure describes how several separate chains assemble, as the four subunits of haemoglobin do.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A mixture of \(o\)-nitrophenol and \(p\)-nitrophenol can be separated by steam distillation.
Reason (R) : \(o\)-nitrophenol is steam volatile due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

The two nitrophenols can indeed be separated by steam distillation, and the ortho isomer is the steam-volatile one — so the Assertion holds.

But the Reason names the wrong kind of hydrogen bonding. In o-nitrophenol the nitro group and the hydroxyl group are close enough to bond to each other WITHIN the same molecule: the bonding is INTRAMOLECULAR, sometimes called chelation. That uses up the hydroxyl's bonding capacity, so the molecules do not associate with one another, and the compound is volatile.

It is p-nitrophenol whose bonding is INTERMOLECULAR — the groups there are too far apart to reach each other, so the molecules associate into larger aggregates, and that compound is the one left behind in the flask. The Reason as written attributes the para isomer's behaviour to the ortho isomer, which reverses the argument.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Cooking time is reduced in pressure cooker.
Reason (R) : Boiling point of water inside the pressure cooker is elevated.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

A pressure cooker works by raising the pressure above the water, and a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure on it. At a higher external pressure the water must be hotter before that happens, so it boils ABOVE \(100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) instead of at it.

The food is therefore cooked at a higher temperature, and reaction rates rise sharply with temperature — so the cooking is finished sooner. The elevation of the boiling point is exactly why the time falls.

The same principle runs the other way on a mountain, where the lower atmospheric pressure makes water boil below \(100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and cooking takes longer.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show irregularities in their electronic configurations.
Reason (R) : Actinoids are radioactive in nature.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Actinoids do show irregularities in their electronic configurations, and they are radioactive throughout the series — both statements are correct.

But the causes are different. The irregularities arise because the \(5f\) and \(6d\) orbitals lie so close in energy that an electron may go into either, so configurations do not follow a tidy pattern. Radioactivity is a property of the NUCLEUS — of an unfavourable ratio of protons to neutrons — and has nothing to do with where the valence electrons sit.

Both facts are consequences of the actinoids being heavy elements, but neither follows from the other.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Vitamin K can be stored in our body.
Reason (R) : Vitamin K is a water soluble vitamin.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Vitamin K can indeed be stored in the body, so the Assertion holds. But the Reason gives the wrong classification: vitamin K is FAT SOLUBLE, not water soluble.

And the correction restores the argument. Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue, which is precisely why the body can keep a reserve of them. WATER-soluble vitamins, the B group and C, are not stored: any excess is excreted in the urine, which is why they must be supplied regularly in the diet.

So the Reason, corrected, would have explained the Assertion; as written it would predict the opposite.

rows.stem: What is meant by positive deviation from Raoult’s law ? Give an example. What type of azeotrope is formed by positive deviation ?
rows.solution:
POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law means the observed vapour pressure of the solution is HIGHER than the value Raoult's law predicts from the mole fractions:
\(p_1 > p_1^{\,\circ}x_1\) and \(p_2 > p_2^{\,\circ}x_2\)

Why it happens. The interactions between UNLIKE molecules in the solution are WEAKER than those between the like molecules of each pure liquid. Held less tightly, the molecules escape into the vapour more readily than expected. Mixing is endothermic and the volume expands slightly — the same fact seen from two other directions.

EXAMPLE: a solution of ethanol and acetone. Pure ethanol is extensively hydrogen bonded to itself; acetone molecules coming between them break some of those bonds and cannot replace them in kind. Carbon disulphide with acetone serves equally well.

TYPE OF AZEOTROPE: a MINIMUM BOILING azeotrope. A higher vapour pressure means a lower boiling point, so the mixture at that composition boils below either pure component. Ethanol and water form one at about 95% ethanol, which is why absolute alcohol cannot be obtained by simple distillation.

rows.stem: State a condition under which a bimolecular reaction is kinetically first order reaction. Give an example. For which type of reactions, do order and molecularity have the same value ?
rows.solution:
CONDITION: a bimolecular reaction becomes kinetically first order when ONE OF THE REACTANTS IS PRESENT IN LARGE EXCESS.

Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds, so it can be treated as a constant and absorbed into the rate constant. What remains depends on one concentration alone, and the reaction is FIRST order in practice though bimolecular by its stoichiometry — a PSEUDO first order reaction.

EXAMPLE: the acid hydrolysis of an ester, where water is also the solvent:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{ester}][\mathrm{H_2O}] = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\)
The inversion of sucrose is another.

WHEN ORDER AND MOLECULARITY AGREE: for an ELEMENTARY reaction — one that takes place in a single step. There the rate law can be read straight off the stoichiometry, because the species that collide are the species in the equation. A complex reaction has no single molecularity at all, and its order is set by the slowest step, which may involve quite different species.

rows.stem: Write the IUPAC name of the complex \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\). Draw the structure of geometrical isomer of this complex which is optically inactive.
rows.solution:
The two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) against an overall charge of \(+2\), and the two ethane-1,2-diamine molecules are neutral, so platinum is \(+4\).

Ligands are named alphabetically, chlorido before the diamine, and the bracketed ligand name takes bis- because its own name already contains a numerical prefix. The complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name:
DICHLORIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)PLATINUM(IV) ION

The optically inactive geometrical isomer is the TRANS form: the two chlorido ligands directly OPPOSITE each other along one axis, with the two chelate rings lying in the plane between them.

That arrangement has a plane of symmetry, so it is superimposable on its mirror image and cannot rotate plane polarised light. The CIS isomer, with the two chlorides adjacent, has no such plane and is chiral — it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the formula of the following coordination compound :
Pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III)chloride
(ii) Write the IUPAC name of the linkage isomer of the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2}\).
rows.solution:
(i) Build the formula from the name. Pentaammine means five \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), carbonato means one \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\), and cobalt is \(+3\). The complex ion therefore carries \(3 - 2 = +1\), which needs ONE chloride outside to balance it:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(CO_3)]Cl}\)

(ii) The nitrite ion is AMBIDENTATE — it can bind through nitrogen or through oxygen — and the complex given is the nitro form, bound through NITROGEN. Its linkage isomer is the one bound through OXYGEN, which is named nitrito-O:
PENTAAMMINENITRITO-O-COBALT(III) CHLORIDE

The two are genuinely different compounds, differing in colour and in stability, though their formulae are written with the same atoms.

rows.stem: Why are haloarenes less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ? How does the presence of nitro \((-\mathrm{NO_2})\) group at ortho- and para-positions in haloarenes increase the reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ?
rows.solution:
WHY HALOARENES ARE LESS REACTIVE. The carbon-halogen bond in a haloarene is far harder to break than in a haloalkane, for two reasons that reinforce each other.

The halogen's lone pair is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond acquires partial DOUBLE BOND character: it is shorter and stronger, and a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute.

And the carbon carrying the halogen is \(sp^2\) hybridised rather than \(sp^3\). An \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character, is more electronegative, and holds the shared pair more tightly.

The electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud of the ring also repels the approaching nucleophile, which is negatively charged.

HOW A NITRO GROUP HELPS. A nitro group at the ORTHO or PARA position is strongly ELECTRON WITHDRAWING. It pulls electron density out of the ring, which makes the ring carbon less repellent to the incoming nucleophile and easier to attack.

More importantly, it stabilises the INTERMEDIATE. Nucleophilic substitution here goes through a negatively charged carbanion, and when the nitro group is ortho or para that negative charge can be delocalised right onto the nitro group's own oxygen. A more stable intermediate means a lower energy barrier and a faster reaction.

The position matters: a nitro group at the META position cannot accept the charge by resonance and has almost no effect. Adding more o- and p-nitro groups helps further, which is why 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water alone.

rows.stem: The two strands in DNA are not identical but complementary. Explain. What products would be formed when DNA is hydrolysed ?
rows.solution:
WHY THE STRANDS ARE COMPLEMENTARY AND NOT IDENTICAL. The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases, and those bonds form only between SPECIFIC PAIRS: adenine always with thymine, through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine always with cytosine, through three.

The pairing is fixed by shape and by the arrangement of donor and acceptor atoms — a larger purine must face a smaller pyrimidine for the strands to stay the right distance apart, and only these two combinations align their hydrogen bonds correctly.

So wherever one strand carries adenine, the other must carry thymine opposite it. The second strand is therefore the MIRROR IMAGE OF THE REQUIREMENT rather than a copy: each strand specifies the other completely, which is exactly what makes replication possible.

ON HYDROLYSIS, DNA gives three kinds of product:
the sugar, \(\beta\)-D-2-DEOXYRIBOSE;
the BASES — adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine;
and PHOSPHORIC ACID.

rows.stem:
\(0{\cdot}3\) g of acetic acid (Molar mass = 60 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) dissolved in 30 g of benzene shows a depression in freezing point equal to \(0{\cdot}45\)°C. Calculate the percentage association of acid if it forms a dimer in the solution.
(Given : \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for benzene = \(5{\cdot}12\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Acetic acid DIMERISES in benzene, so fewer particles are present than the formula suggests and the van't Hoff factor comes out BELOW 1.

Step 1 — the observed factor. Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{i\,K_f \times w_2 \times 1000}{M_2 \times w_1}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = \dfrac{i \times 5{\cdot}12 \times 0{\cdot}3 \times 1000}{60 \times 30}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = i \times 0{\cdot}8533\)
\(i = 0{\cdot}527\)

Step 2 — degree of association. Two molecules combine into one dimer, so \(n = 2\) and
\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{\frac{1}{n} - 1} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}527 - 1}{\frac{1}{2} - 1} = \dfrac{-0{\cdot}473}{-0{\cdot}5}\)
\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}945\)

Percentage association \(= 94{\cdot}5\%\) — rounding \(i\) to three figures before the last step returns \(94{\cdot}6\%\), which is the same answer to the precision the data allow.

The sign of the deviation is the check on the whole calculation. Association REDUCES the particle count, so \(i < 1\) and the observed depression is SMALLER than the formula predicts. Dissociation would have done the opposite.

rows.stem: Write the name of the cell which is generally used in inverters. Write the reactions taking place at anode and cathode of this cell, when it is in use.
rows.solution:
The cell used in inverters is the LEAD STORAGE BATTERY.

It is a secondary cell — one that can be recharged — built from a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide as the cathode, both dipping in about 38% sulphuric acid.

AT THE ANODE, lead is oxidised and the lead(II) formed is at once precipitated as the insoluble sulphate:
\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^-\)

AT THE CATHODE, lead dioxide is reduced, also ending as lead sulphate:
\(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

Both electrodes therefore become coated with lead sulphate as the cell discharges, and the acid is consumed — which is why a discharged battery can be recognised from the fall in the density of its electrolyte. On recharging, an external voltage drives both reactions backwards.

rows.stem:
Explain why electrolysis of an aqueous solution of NaCl gives \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas at cathode and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas at anode ? Write overall reaction.
(Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Na^{+}/Na}} = -2{\cdot}71\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{H_2O/H_2}} = -0{\cdot}83\) V,
\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cl_2/2Cl^{-}}} = +1{\cdot}36\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{H^{+}/O_2/H_2O}} = +1{\cdot}23\) V)
rows.solution:
AT THE CATHODE the two candidates for reduction are the sodium ion and water:
\(\mathrm{Na^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}\), \(E^{\circ} = -2{\cdot}71\) V
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\), \(E^{\circ} = -0{\cdot}83\) V

The species with the HIGHER reduction potential is reduced preferentially, and \(-0{\cdot}83\) is far higher than \(-2{\cdot}71\). Water is reduced, hydrogen gas is evolved, and the sodium ion stays in solution.

AT THE ANODE the comparison alone would predict the opposite of what happens:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\), \(E^{\circ} = +1{\cdot}23\) V
\(2\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2e^-\), \(E^{\circ} = +1{\cdot}36\) V

The lower potential is the easier oxidation, so on these figures water should be oxidised. It is not — and the reason is OVERPOTENTIAL. Liberating oxygen at an electrode requires a substantial extra voltage beyond its thermodynamic value, whereas chlorine needs almost none. That extra requirement more than wipes out the \(0{\cdot}13\) V advantage, and CHLORINE is evolved instead.

OVERALL REACTION:
\(\mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^-(aq)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}\)

The sodium and hydroxide ions left in solution are sodium hydroxide, which is why this electrolysis is the industrial source of all three of caustic soda, chlorine and hydrogen. Note that the anode here is the one case in this syllabus where the potentials alone give the wrong answer.

rows.stem:
The following data were obtained during the first order thermal decomposition of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5\,(g)}\) at constant volume :
\(\mathrm{2N_2O_5\,(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{2N_2O_4\,(g)} + \mathrm{O_2\,(g)}\)

| S.No. | Time/s | Total Pressure/atm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | \(0{\cdot}5\) |
| 2 | 100 | \(0{\cdot}625\) |

Calculate rate constant.
[ Given : log 2 = \(0{\cdot}3010\), log 10 = 1 ]
rows.solution:
Only the TOTAL pressure was measured, so the first task is to recover the pressure of the reactant from it.

Set up the pressures. Let the initial pressure of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) be \(p_i\) and let \(x\) atm of oxygen have formed at time \(t\). The equation shows that making \(x\) of oxygen consumes \(2x\) of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) and produces \(2x\) of \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\):

\(p_{\text{total}} = (p_i - 2x) + 2x + x = p_i + x\)

so \(x = p_{\text{total}} - p_i\), and the pressure of the reactant is
\(p_{\mathrm{A}} = p_i - 2x = p_i - 2(p_{\text{total}} - p_i) = 3p_i - 2p_{\text{total}}\)

Put in the numbers at \(t = 100\) s:
\(p_{\mathrm{A}} = (3 \times 0{\cdot}5) - (2 \times 0{\cdot}625) = 1{\cdot}5 - 1{\cdot}25 = 0{\cdot}25\) atm

Apply the first order equation. Pressure may be used in place of concentration, since the two are proportional at constant volume and temperature and the ratio is all that enters:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_{\mathrm{A}}} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{100}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{0{\cdot}25}\)
\(= \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{100} \times \log 2 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{100} \times 0{\cdot}3010\)

\(k = 6{\cdot}93 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

A useful check: the reactant pressure has fallen exactly to half its starting value in 100 s, so 100 s is the half-life, and \(k = 0{\cdot}693/100\) gives the same answer in one line.

rows.stem: A compound (A) with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_9I}\) which is a primary alkyl halide, reacts with alcoholic KOH to give compound (B). Compound (B) reacts with HI to give (C) which is an isomer of (A). When (A) reacts with Na metal in the presence of dry ether, it gives a compound (D), \(\mathrm{C_8H_{18}}\), which is different from the compound formed when n-butyl iodide reacts with sodium. Write the structures of (A), (B), (C) and (D). Write the chemical equation when compound (A) is reacted with alcoholic KOH.
rows.solution:
Take the clues in turn.

Compound \(\mathrm{A}\) is \(\mathrm{C_4H_9I}\) and PRIMARY, which allows only two structures — n-butyl iodide or isobutyl iodide. The last clue settles it: the Wurtz product \(\mathrm{D}\) must be DIFFERENT from the one n-butyl iodide gives, so \(\mathrm{A}\) is the branched one.
\(\mathrm{A} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCH_2I}\), 1-iodo-2-methylpropane

Alcoholic potassium hydroxide ELIMINATES, giving the alkene:
\(\mathrm{B} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2}\), 2-methylpropene

Adding hydrogen iodide back to that alkene follows Markovnikov's rule, so the iodine goes to the MORE substituted carbon — a different carbon from where it started, which is why \(\mathrm{C}\) is an isomer of \(\mathrm{A}\) rather than \(\mathrm{A}\) itself:
\(\mathrm{C} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CI}\), 2-iodo-2-methylpropane

Sodium in dry ether couples two molecules of \(\mathrm{A}\) end to end:
\(\mathrm{D} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)_2}\), 2,5-dimethylhexane

That is \(\mathrm{C_8H_{18}}\) as required, and it is indeed different from the n-octane that n-butyl iodide would have given — which is the clue that fixed \(\mathrm{A}\) in the first place.

Equation asked for:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHCH_2I} + \mathrm{KOH(alc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KI} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
Write structure of the products of the following reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OCH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \text{conc. } \mathrm{HNO_3} \longrightarrow\)
(c) \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-MgBr} + \mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^{+}/H_2O}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — all three starting materials are printed as DRAWN 2-D structures rather than formulas: (a) a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{OCH_3}\) (anisole), (b) a benzene ring bearing OH (phenol), (c) a cyclohexane ring bearing MgBr (cyclohexylmagnesium bromide). NAMED, not described: these are the REACTANTS of a 'write the product' question, so reading them losslessly as formulas cannot state the answer. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) Cleaving an ether with hydrogen iodide always breaks the bond on the side that can accept the iodide. Here one side is an ARYL group, and an aryl-oxygen bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring — it will not break. So the iodide attacks the METHYL carbon instead:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}OCH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)
The products are PHENOL and IODOMETHANE.

(b) Concentrated nitric acid nitrates phenol at all three activated positions:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH}\)
The product is 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL, picric acid.

(c) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and with METHANAL — the only aldehyde with two hydrogens on that carbon — the product after hydrolysis is a PRIMARY alcohol with one carbon more than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}MgBr} + \mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}/\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}CH_2OH}\)
The product is CYCLOHEXYLMETHANOL. Any other aldehyde would have given a secondary alcohol, and a ketone a tertiary one.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(b) HCHO is more reactive than \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) towards addition of HCN.
(c) Vinyl group directly attached with carboxylic acid should decrease the acidity of corresponding carboxylic acid due to resonance, but on the contrary it increases the acidity.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the carboxyl group DEACTIVATES the ring and, worse, destroys the catalyst.

The carboxyl group withdraws electron density from the benzene ring, so the ring is poor at attacking an electrophile — the opposite of what a Friedel-Crafts reaction needs. And the catalyst, aluminium chloride, is a Lewis acid: it bonds to the lone pair on the carboxyl oxygen, forming a complex. The catalyst is thereby tied up, and the group it is attached to withdraws electrons more strongly still.

(b) Because the carbonyl carbon of methanal is MORE ELECTROPHILIC.

Addition of hydrogen cyanide begins with the cyanide ion attacking that carbon, so the more positive it is, the faster the reaction. Ethanal carries a methyl group there, and a methyl group RELEASES electron density by its inductive effect, reducing the positive charge. Methanal has only hydrogens, which do not.

The methyl group also gets in the way sterically, crowding the carbon the nucleophile must reach. Both effects point the same way, and both grow with each further alkyl group — which is why ketones are less reactive still.

(c) Because the resonance argument is outweighed by the INDUCTIVE one, and the inductive effect here belongs to an \(sp^2\) carbon.

The carbon of a vinyl group is \(sp^2\) hybridised, and an \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character than an \(sp^3\) one, holds its electrons closer to the nucleus and is therefore more ELECTRONEGATIVE. It withdraws electron density from the carboxyl group, stabilising the carboxylate ion left behind after the proton leaves.

A more stable anion means a stronger acid. So although resonance donation would, taken alone, reduce the acidity, the electron-withdrawing inductive effect of the \(sp^2\) carbon is the stronger of the two and the acidity rises instead.

rows.stem:
Write the reaction of D-Glucose with the following :
(a) HCN
(b) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
(c) \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN CYANIDE, glucose forms a CYANOHYDRIN — hydrogen cyanide adds across the aldehyde group, the cyanide to the carbon and the hydrogen to the oxygen. The product has one carbon more than the sugar:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH(OH)(CN)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
That this addition works at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a carbonyl group.

(b) WITH BROMINE WATER, glucose is oxidised to a six carbon carboxylic acid, GLUCONIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}\text{ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
Bromine water is too MILD to attack a hydroxyl group, so this reaction proves specifically that the group oxidised was an ALDEHYDE.

(c) WITH ACETIC ANHYDRIDE, glucose is acetylated to GLUCOSE PENTAACETATE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
Five acetyl groups go on, and each needs a hydroxyl group to attach to — which is how the FIVE hydroxyl groups of glucose are counted.

rows.stem:
On the basis of CFT, explain why \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\) complex is coloured ? What happens on heating the complex \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\) ? Give reason.
[Atomic no. : Ti = 22]
rows.context: The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d-orbital splitting is smaller as compared to the octahedral entity.
rows.solution:
Titanium is atomic number 22, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^2 4s^2\). In \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\) the three chlorides outside the sphere give \(-3\) and the six water molecules are neutral, so titanium is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\).

WHY IT IS COLOURED. The six water ligands split the five d orbitals into a lower \(t_{2g}\) set and an upper \(e_g\) set. The single d electron sits in \(t_{2g}\), and it can absorb a photon of visible light and jump to \(e_g\) — a d-d transition, \(t_{2g}^1 \longrightarrow e_g^1\).

The energy absorbed corresponds to the yellow-green region, so what is TRANSMITTED is the complementary colour, and the solution looks violet.

WHAT HAPPENS ON HEATING. The colour fades and the compound becomes COLOURLESS.

Heating drives off the water ligands. Without ligands there is no crystal field, so the five d orbitals return to being degenerate; with no splitting there is no gap for the electron to jump across, no visible light is absorbed, and no colour remains.

rows.stem: What is crystal field splitting energy ?
rows.context: The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d-orbital splitting is smaller as compared to the octahedral entity.
rows.solution:
CRYSTAL FIELD SPLITTING ENERGY is the ENERGY DIFFERENCE between the two sets of d orbitals that the ligands create.

In a free metal ion the five d orbitals are degenerate — all of the same energy. Bring ligands up to it and their negative charge repels the d electrons, but unequally: the orbitals pointing straight at the ligands are raised more than those pointing between them. In an octahedral field the set splits into a lower \(t_{2g}\) group of three and an upper \(e_g\) group of two, and the gap between them is written \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\).

Its size depends on the ligand — which is what the spectrochemical series orders — and on the metal's oxidation state. It is \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) that a d-d transition must cross, so it determines the colour, and comparing it with the pairing energy determines the magnetic behaviour.

rows.stem: On the basis of \(\Delta_o\) and P (pairing energy), how can you differentiate between a strong field ligand and a weak field ligand ?
rows.context: The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d-orbital splitting is smaller as compared to the octahedral entity.
rows.solution:
Compare the splitting energy \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) with the PAIRING ENERGY \(\mathrm{P}\), the energy cost of forcing two electrons into the same orbital. Electrons take whichever course is cheaper.

If \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\), climbing to the upper set costs less than pairing, so electrons spread out singly over all five orbitals. The ligand is a WEAK FIELD ligand, and the complex is HIGH SPIN.

If \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\), pairing is the cheaper of the two, so electrons fill the lower set completely before any goes up. The ligand is a STRONG FIELD ligand, and the complex is LOW SPIN.

The consequence is measurable: the weak field complex keeps more unpaired electrons and is the more strongly paramagnetic of the two.

rows.stem: Why are low spin tetrahedral complexes rarely observed ?
rows.context: The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d-orbital splitting is smaller as compared to the octahedral entity.
rows.solution:
Because a TETRAHEDRAL field splits the d orbitals only weakly, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}}\) is almost never large enough to force pairing.

Two things work against it. A tetrahedral complex has only FOUR ligands rather than six, so there is less repulsion to do the splitting; and none of those ligands points directly at a d orbital, so the splitting they do produce is less efficient. The result is that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}}\) is only about four-ninths of \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) for the same metal and ligands.

That figure is essentially always below the pairing energy. With \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} < \mathrm{P}\) the electrons always prefer to occupy the upper orbitals singly rather than pair up, so tetrahedral complexes are high spin, and low spin ones are hardly ever seen.

rows.stem:
How can you convert the following ?
(i) Ethanoic acid to methanamine
(ii) Propanenitrile to 1-aminopropane
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from amides, imides, halides, nitro compounds, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and H-bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. Amines being basic in nature, react with acids to form salts. Aryldiazonium salts, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to produce aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
(i) ETHANOIC ACID TO METHANAMINE, in two steps. Note that the product has ONE CARBON FEWER than the acid, which is the signature of the Hofmann degradation and tells you which route to take.

First convert the acid to its amide by heating with ammonia:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\)

Then degrade the amide with bromine in alkali:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(ii) PROPANENITRILE TO 1-AMINOPROPANE, in one step. Here the carbon count is UNCHANGED — three in, three out — so the nitrile is simply reduced rather than degraded:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2C{\equiv}N} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2}/\mathrm{Pt}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)
Lithium aluminium hydride, or sodium in ethanol, would serve equally well.

The pair of conversions is a lesson in counting carbons before choosing a method.

rows.stem: Why is \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) value of aniline more than that of methylamine ?
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from amides, imides, halides, nitro compounds, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and H-bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. Amines being basic in nature, react with acids to form salts. Aryldiazonium salts, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to produce aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
A higher \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, so the question is asking why aniline is the weaker of the two.

In ANILINE the nitrogen's lone pair is not confined to the nitrogen. It is delocalised INTO THE BENZENE RING by resonance, spread over the ortho and para carbons, so it is less available to accept a proton. The nitrogen is also attached to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which is more electronegative than an \(sp^3\) one and pulls density away from it as well.

In METHYLAMINE there is no ring to absorb the lone pair, and the methyl group RELEASES electron density towards the nitrogen, making that pair still more available.

A less available lone pair means a weaker base and a larger \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) — about 9.4 for aniline against about 3.4 for methylamine, a difference of six orders of magnitude.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in increasing order of their basic strength in aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2},\ \mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH},\ \mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\)
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from amides, imides, halides, nitro compounds, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and H-bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. Amines being basic in nature, react with acids to form salts. Aryldiazonium salts, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to produce aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
Increasing basic strength in AQUEOUS solution:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH}\)

The order is not a simple progression, because three effects compete. Methyl groups RELEASE electron density onto the nitrogen, which would favour the tertiary amine. But the cation formed on protonation must be STABILISED BY HYDROGEN BONDING to the surrounding water, and that needs hydrogens on the nitrogen — the tertiary amine's cation has only one. Its three methyl groups also crowd the water away.

The secondary amine is the compromise that wins: two methyl groups pushing electrons in, and still one hydrogen available for solvation. The tertiary amine comes last on both solvation counts.

The qualification "in aqueous solution" is load-bearing. In the GAS PHASE there is no solvent to stabilise anything, only the inductive effect operates, and the order becomes simply primary, secondary, tertiary.

rows.stem:
Give the structures of A and B in the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe/HCl}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{273\ K}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{B}\)
rows.context: Amines are usually formed from amides, imides, halides, nitro compounds, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and H-bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. Amines being basic in nature, react with acids to form salts. Aryldiazonium salts, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to produce aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group — the standard laboratory preparation of aniline, preferred industrially because the iron is regenerated by the acid:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid at 273 K then diazotises it. Aniline is an AROMATIC primary amine, so unlike an aliphatic one its diazonium salt survives at this temperature — the ring stabilises it by delocalising the positive charge:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

The low temperature is essential. Above about 278 K the salt decomposes, the nitrogen leaves as a gas, and the product is phenol instead.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(I) The \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) value for manganese is highly negative, whereas \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}}\) is highly positive.
(II) Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
(III) Transition metals have high melting points.
(ii) Complete the following ionic equations :
(I) \(\mathrm{5SO_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{2MnO_4^{-}} + \mathrm{6H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
(II) \(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^{-}} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(i)(I) The two potentials describe different things, and each is set by the stability of \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\).

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) is highly NEGATIVE because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell, and therefore unusually stable. Manganese metal gives up two electrons readily to reach it, so the metal is easily oxidised and the reduction potential is correspondingly negative.

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}}\) is highly POSITIVE for the very same reason, seen from the other side. \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is \(3d^4\) and would gain that stable half-filled configuration by picking up one electron, so it is strongly inclined to be reduced — which is exactly what a large positive potential means. Manganese(III) is accordingly a powerful oxidising agent.

(II) Because the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals of the actinoids lie at COMPARABLE ENERGIES. Electrons from all three sets are therefore available for bonding, and there is no strong preference for stopping at any one number — uranium runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\), and neptunium and plutonium reach \(+7\).

The lanthanoids are the contrast: there the \(4f\) orbitals are buried well below the valence level and take no part, so nearly all lanthanoids are restricted to \(+3\).

(III) Because in a transition metal the \((n-1)d\) electrons take part in the metallic bonding ALONGSIDE the \(ns\) electrons.

A greater number of electrons involved in the interatomic bonding means stronger metallic bonding, and melting a metal means overcoming exactly that. The effect peaks in the middle of the series, where the unpaired d electrons are most numerous, and falls away at zinc, whose full d subshell contributes nothing — which is why zinc melts at a mere 693 K against chromium's 2130 K.

(ii)(I) Permanganate oxidises sulphite to sulphate in acid, manganese falling from \(+7\) to \(+2\):
\(5\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 6\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)
Ten electrons change hands, five sulphites giving up two each and two permanganates taking five each.

(II) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution permanganate goes only as far as manganese dioxide, and iodide is oxidised to iodate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} + \mathrm{IO_3^-}\)
Here six electrons change hands: manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+4\), three each, while iodine climbs from \(-1\) to \(+5\).

The pair shows how the MEDIUM decides the product — acid takes permanganate to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), neutral solution only to \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Name two elements of 3d series for which the third ionisation enthalpies are quite high.
(ii) Out of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), which one is paramagnetic and why ?
(iii) Write any one consequence of lanthanoid contraction.
(iv) How do you prepare potassium manganate from pyrolusite ore ?
(v) Why is the ability of oxygen more than fluorine to stabilise higher oxidation states of transition metals ?
rows.solution:
(i) MANGANESE and ZINC. Nickel and copper would serve equally well.

The third ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove an electron from the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion, so it is high wherever that ion has a specially stable configuration. \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\), an exactly half-filled subshell; \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\), completely filled. Both resist losing a further electron strongly.

(ii) POTASSIUM MANGANATE, \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), is the paramagnetic one.

Work out the oxidation state in each. In \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) the two potassiums give \(+2\) and four oxides \(-8\), so manganese is \(+6\) and \(\mathrm{Mn^{6+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — ONE unpaired electron, hence paramagnetic. In \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) manganese is \(+7\) and the ion is \(3d^0\) — no d electron at all, so nothing to be unpaired, and it is diamagnetic.

The colour of permanganate is therefore NOT a d-d transition; it comes from charge transfer, oxygen to metal.

(iii) The 4d and 5d series elements have almost IDENTICAL ATOMIC RADII — zirconium and hafnium, or niobium and tantalum, are famously hard to tell apart and notoriously hard to separate. The contraction across the intervening f-block cancels the increase the extra period would otherwise bring.

A second consequence: the lanthanoids themselves are very similar in size and so very similar in chemistry, which is why separating them is difficult.

(iv) POTASSIUM MANGANATE FROM PYROLUSITE. Pyrolusite is manganese dioxide. Fuse it with an alkali metal hydroxide in the presence of an oxidising agent — air will do, or potassium nitrate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Manganese is oxidised from \(+4\) to \(+6\), and the dark green manganate is formed.

(v) Because OXYGEN CAN FORM MULTIPLE BONDS with the metal while fluorine cannot.

Oxygen has two lone pairs available for donation into the metal's empty d orbitals, so an \(\mathrm{M{=}O}\) bond carries \(\pi\) character on top of its \(\sigma\) bond, and that extra bonding stabilises a metal in a very high oxidation state. Fluorine forms only a single \(\sigma\) bond.

The evidence is in the compounds: manganese reaches \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) but only \(+4\) in its highest fluoride, and osmium reaches \(+8\) in \(\mathrm{OsO_4}\).

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) An organic compound (X) having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) can show various properties depending on its structures. Draw each of the structures if it :
(I) shows Cannizzaro reaction.
(II) reduces Tollens’ reagent and has a chiral carbon.
(III) gives positive iodoform test.
(ii) Write the reaction involved in the following :
(I) Clemmensen reduction
(II) Etard reaction
rows.solution:
(i) The formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) has one degree of unsaturation, which the carbonyl group uses up — so every structure below is a saturated aldehyde or ketone with five carbons.

(I) CANNIZZARO REACTION requires an aldehyde with NO \(\alpha\)-HYDROGEN, since an aldehyde that has one undergoes aldol instead. The carbon next to the carbonyl must therefore carry no hydrogen at all, which means it must be fully substituted:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO}\), 2,2-dimethylpropanal

(II) REDUCES TOLLENS' REAGENT means it is an ALDEHYDE; a chiral carbon means one carbon must carry four different groups. Putting the methyl branch on the second carbon does both:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3){-}CHO}\), 2-methylbutanal
Its second carbon holds a methyl, an ethyl, a hydrogen and the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group — four different things.

(III) POSITIVE IODOFORM TEST means a METHYL group attached to the carbonyl carbon:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_2CH_2CH_3}\), pentan-2-one

(ii)(I) CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), using zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{Zn\text{-}Hg}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
It is the acidic counterpart of Wolff-Kishner reduction, which does the same job in alkali — the choice between them is decided by what else in the molecule would survive.

(II) ETARD REACTION oxidises the methyl group of toluene to an aldehyde and stops there. Chromyl chloride in carbon disulphide forms a chromium complex that protects the product; hydrolysis then releases it:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OCrOHCl_2)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)
The intermediate complex is the whole point: without it the oxidation would run on to benzoic acid.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Draw structure of the methyl hemiacetal of methanal.
(ii) There are two \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups in semicarbazide. However only one is involved in the formation of semicarbazones. Give reason.
(iii) How will you convert ethanol to 3-hydroxybutanal ?
(iv) Complete the following equation :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}}\) ?
(v) Write the final product formed when phthalic acid is treated with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) followed by strong heating.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (iv)'s starting material is printed as a DRAWN cyclohexane ring bearing OH, read here losslessly as \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-OH}\) (cyclohexanol). NAMED, not described: it is the reactant of a 'complete the equation' question, so reading it as a formula cannot state the answer. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) A hemiacetal is what an alcohol gives on adding ONCE to a carbonyl group — the carbon ends up carrying both an \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and an \(-\mathrm{OR}\). Methanal has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, so with methanol:
\(\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{CH_3OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2C(OH)(OCH_3)}\)
The structure is a carbon bearing two hydrogens, one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and one \(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\). A second molecule of methanol would carry it on to the acetal.

(ii) Because one of the two amino groups is DEACTIVATED BY RESONANCE.

Semicarbazide is \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2}\), and one of its \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups is attached DIRECTLY to the carbonyl carbon. That nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen, so it is not available for attacking anything — it is an amide nitrogen, and amide nitrogens are poor nucleophiles.

The other \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), the terminal one, is separated from the carbonyl by an intervening nitrogen and takes no part in that delocalisation. Its lone pair is free, so it is the one that attacks the aldehyde or ketone and forms the semicarbazone.

(iii) ETHANOL TO 3-HYDROXYBUTANAL, in two steps. Count carbons first: two in, four out, so a coupling is needed — and a hydroxyl beta to an aldehyde is the signature of an ALDOL ADDITION.

Oxidise the ethanol to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

Then treat with dilute alkali WITHOUT heating, so the addition stops at the \(\beta\)-hydroxy aldehyde:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\)
Heating would dehydrate it to but-2-enal, so the mild condition is essential.

(iv) Chromium trioxide oxidises a SECONDARY alcohol to a ketone, and cyclohexanol is secondary:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_{10}{=}O}\)
The product is CYCLOHEXANONE — the ring unchanged, with a \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) where the \(\mathrm{CH{-}OH}\) was.

(v) Ammonia converts phthalic acid to its ammonium salt and then to the diamide; strong heating drives ammonia out from between the two amide groups, closing a five-membered ring:
phthalic acid \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_3}}\) benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide \(\xrightarrow{\text{strong heating}}\) PHTHALIMIDE
a ring carrying \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\), \(\mathrm{NH}\) and \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) fused to the benzene ring.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the emf of the following cell at 25°C :
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\ (0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{H^{+}}\ (0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{H_2(g)}\ (1\ \mathrm{bar}),\ \mathrm{Pt(s)}\)
[ Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0{\cdot}76\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{2H^{+}/H_2}} = 0{\cdot}00\) V, log 10 = 1 ]
(ii) State Faraday’s second law of electrolysis. How much electricity is required in terms of Faraday for the reduction of 1 mol of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so zinc is oxidised, and the hydrogen electrode on the right is the cathode.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}00 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid zinc does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10^{3}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 3 = 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0885\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}6715\ \mathrm{V}\), or \(0{\cdot}67\) V

Note the squared term. Halving the hydrogen ion concentration would change the quotient FOUR-fold, not two — a point the arithmetic here makes concrete, since \(0{\cdot}1/0{\cdot}0001\) is a thousand rather than ten.

(ii) FARADAY'S SECOND LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS. When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes, the amounts of the different substances liberated at the electrodes are proportional to their CHEMICAL EQUIVALENT WEIGHTS.

For the reduction asked about, count the change in oxidation state. In \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) the seven oxides give \(-14\) against an overall \(-2\), so the two chromiums share \(+12\) and each is \(+6\); in \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) each is \(+3\). Each chromium therefore gains THREE electrons, and there are TWO of them:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

One mole of dichromate needs 6 mol of electrons, that is 6 FARADAY. Answering 3 F is the trap — that figure belongs to one mole of chromium, not one mole of the dichromate ion.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) The conductivity of \(0{\cdot}20\) M solution of KCl is \(2{\cdot}48 \times 10^{-2}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation \((\alpha)\).
[Given : \(\lambda^{\circ}_{(\mathrm{K^{+}})} = 73{\cdot}5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\lambda^{\circ}_{(\mathrm{Cl^{-}})} = 76{\cdot}5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)]
(ii) Calculate \(\Delta_r\mathrm{G^{\circ}}\) of the following cell :
\(\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)
[Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = -2{\cdot}37\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} = +0{\cdot}34\) V
1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
(iii) What type of cell is mercury cell ? Why is it more advantageous than dry cell ?
rows.solution:
(i) MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY. Conductivity is a property of a fixed volume; molar conductivity refers it to one mole of electrolyte, so the concentration divides out:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}48 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}20}\)
\(\Lambda_m = 124\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION. At infinite dilution the electrolyte is fully dissociated, and by Kohlrausch's law the limiting value is the sum of the two ionic contributions:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{K^+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}} = 73{\cdot}5 + 76{\cdot}5 = 150\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{124}{150} = 0{\cdot}827\)

(ii) Magnesium has the more negative potential, so it is the anode and copper the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}34 - (-2{\cdot}37) = 2{\cdot}71\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -2 \times 96500 \times 2{\cdot}71\)

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -523030\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} = -523{\cdot}03\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The sign is the check: a positive cell potential must give a negative free energy change, which is what makes the reaction spontaneous.

(iii) The mercury cell is a PRIMARY cell — its reaction is not reversible, so it cannot be recharged and is discarded once exhausted.

Its ADVANTAGE over the dry cell is a CONSTANT POTENTIAL throughout its life, about \(1{\cdot}35\) V. The reason is structural: its overall reaction, zinc with mercury(II) oxide giving zinc oxide and mercury, involves no ion in solution whose concentration can change, so there is nothing in the Nernst quotient to shift. The dry cell's reaction does produce and consume ions in its paste, so its voltage falls steadily as it is used.

A steady voltage makes the mercury cell suited to hearing aids and watches, where a drifting supply would be a nuisance.
